title: Gravity & Falling Objects
keyIdea: Gravity is a pulling force between the Earth and every object. It pulls things towards the centre of the Earth all the time. A book on a table does not fall because the table pushes up just as hard. Take the support away and the object is unsupported, so it falls. Heavy and light objects fall at the same rate; only air resistance slows wide, light things like feathers. Weight is the pull of gravity, measured in newtons: about 10 N for each kilogram.
familyTip: Hold a book and a sheet of paper at the same height and let go: the book wins. Now scrunch the paper into a tight ball and try again. They land together, because only the air was slowing the flat sheet. Ask what is holding up each thing in the room.

visual.caption: Is something holding it up? Drag each card into a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: an apple that has come off its branch
a lamp hanging on a string
a ball rolling off the edge of a table

lab.caption: Flagship lab: show the forces on held-up objects, take the supports away, race heavy against light, drop balls round the globe and weigh masses.

kid: Gravity is a force. It is a pull between the Earth and every object. It pulls things towards the Earth, even when they are not moving. It is why you come back down when you jump, and why rain runs downhill.

A book on a table does not fall. Gravity pulls it down, but the table pushes it up just as hard. The two forces balance. Take the table away and the book is unsupported. Now only gravity acts, so the book falls. It gets faster as it falls.

Heavy things do not fall faster. Drop a big and a small ball of the same size together and they land at the same time. A feather is slow because air pushes up on it. With no air, a feather and a hammer land together. An astronaut showed this on the Moon in 1971.

The Earth is a ball, so gravity pulls towards its middle. That is why people in Australia do not fall off. Weight is the pull of gravity. We measure it in newtons with a forcemeter. One kilogram weighs about 10 newtons on Earth.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. This matches Year 5 Forces in the National Curriculum in England (explain that unsupported objects fall towards the Earth because of the force of gravity acting between the Earth and the falling object) and NGSS 5-PS2-1 (support an argument that the gravitational force exerted by Earth on objects is directed down). It builds on Contact & Non-Contact Forces, Forces Vocabulary and Drawing Force Diagrams, and leads into air resistance and mass versus weight.

Gravity is a non-contact force of attraction between any two masses; the Earth's pull on nearby objects is what we call weight. On Earth the gravitational field strength is about 9.8 N/kg, rounded to 10 N/kg at this age. A heavier object is pulled harder but has proportionally more mass to accelerate, so without air resistance every object falls with the same acceleration. 'Down' means towards the centre of the Earth.

Common mistakes: thinking gravity only acts on falling things, so a resting book has no forces on it. Believing heavier objects fall much faster, which air resistance on light, wide objects seems to confirm. Thinking air pushes things down. Imagining 'down' as the bottom of a map, so people on the far side of the globe would fall off. And mixing up mass, in kilograms, with weight, a force in newtons.

In the lab your child shows the balanced forces on a book, a lamp and a ball, then takes each support away and watches them fall. They race a heavy and a light ball, then a feather and a ball with and without air. Then they drop balls from people all round a globe and hang masses on a forcemeter.

practice.prompt: A book rests on a table. Which statement is true?
choices: gravity pulls it down and the table pushes it up just as hard
no forces act on it because it is still
gravity switches off while it is on the table
practice.hint: Does gravity stop when something stops moving?
practice.explain: Gravity still pulls the book down. The table pushes up with the same size of force, so the forces balance and the book stays still.

practice.prompt: A 4 kg ball and a 1 kg ball, the same size, are dropped from the same height at the same time. What happens?
choices: they land at almost the same time
the 4 kg ball lands much sooner
the 1 kg ball lands first
practice.hint: Air resistance is about the same on two balls of the same size.
practice.explain: Gravity makes all objects speed up at the same rate. With the same size and shape, air slows them about the same, so they land together.

practice.prompt: On Earth, 1 kg weighs about 10 N. About how many newtons does a {a} kg bag weigh?
practice.hint: Multiply the mass in kilograms by 10.
practice.explain: {a} kg × 10 N per kg = {=10*a} N. More mass means a bigger pull from gravity.

practice.prompt: A forcemeter shows that a box weighs {=10*a} N on Earth. About what is its mass in kilograms?
practice.hint: Each kilogram weighs about 10 N, so divide by 10.
practice.explain: {=10*a} N ÷ 10 N per kg = {a} kg. Weight is the force in newtons; mass is the amount of stuff in kilograms.

practice.prompt: A girl in New Zealand, on the far side of the Earth from the UK, drops her pencil. Which way does it fall?
choices: towards the ground at her feet, towards the Earth's centre
up, away from the Earth
sideways
practice.hint: Gravity pulls towards the centre of the Earth.
practice.explain: Down means towards the centre of the Earth wherever you stand, so her pencil falls to the ground just as it would in the UK.

pool.prompt: Why does an apple fall when it comes off a tree?
choices: gravity pulls it towards the Earth
the air pushes it down
heavy things want to go down
pool.hint: Which force acts between the Earth and every object?
pool.explain: Once nothing supports it, gravity, the pull between the Earth and the apple, makes it fall.

pool.prompt: A flat sheet of paper falls more slowly than a book. Why?
choices: air resistance slows the wide, light sheet much more
gravity does not pull on paper
paper is too light to fall
pool.hint: What happens if you scrunch the paper into a ball?
pool.explain: Air pushes up on the wide sheet. Scrunched into a ball, it falls almost as fast as the book. Gravity pulls on both.

pool.prompt: A lamp hangs from the ceiling on a cord. Which forces act on it?
choices: gravity down and the cord pulling up
only the cord pulling up
no forces, because it is not moving
pool.hint: Something must balance the pull of gravity.
pool.explain: Gravity pulls the lamp down and the cord pulls up just as hard, so the forces balance. Cut the cord and it falls.

choices: newtons, because weight is a force
kilograms, like mass
metres
pool.hint: Weight is the pull of gravity. What unit is used for forces?
pool.explain: Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons with a forcemeter. Mass is measured in kilograms.

pool.prompt: A dog has a mass of {a} kg. About how much does it weigh on Earth, in newtons?
pool.explain: Each kilogram is pulled with about 10 N, so {a} kg × 10 N per kg = {=10*a} N. Its mass stays {a} kg; its weight is {=10*a} N.

pool.prompt: Two bags hang on forcemeters. One reads {=10*a} N and the other reads {=10*b} N. About how many kilograms heavier is the first bag?
pool.hint: Turn each reading into kilograms by dividing by 10, then subtract.
pool.explain: {=10*a} N is about {a} kg and {=10*b} N is about {b} kg, so the first bag is about {=a-b} kg heavier.

pool.prompt: On the Moon there is no air. An astronaut drops a hammer and a feather together. What happens?
choices: they land at the same time
the hammer lands first
the feather floats away
pool.hint: What slows a feather on Earth?
pool.explain: With no air resistance, gravity makes both speed up at the same rate, so they land together. Astronaut David Scott did this in 1971.

pool.prompt: Rain falls on a hillside. Where does the water go?
choices: downhill, pulled by gravity
uphill to the top
it stays exactly where it lands
pool.explain: Gravity pulls the water down the slope, so it runs downhill into streams, lakes and the sea.
